source.title_on_document: Human-AI Collaboration for Brainstorming: Effect of the Presence of AI Ideas on Breadth of Exploration

supplement.holds: No supplement or appendix is referenced or included in this PDF. The earlier study described as under review is a separate study report, not an identified supplement (PDF pp. 1 and 4). Main-text results contain tests and a rank-biserial correlation, but no arm SDs, SEs, or confidence intervals for the main contrasts.

paper_design_summary: This paper reanalyzes a randomized brainstorming experiment conducted in university informatics courses; 52 students were analyzed after two exclusions, with 26 per arm (PDF pp. 1, 4–5, sections 1, 3.1 and 4). Students generated food-waste reduction ideas individually with or without on-demand GPT-3.5 suggestions, and a condition-blind assistant categorized their output to score category breadth and fluency (PDF pp. 4–6, sections 3.1–4.1). Additional descriptive analyses compare the pooled category profiles and new-category contributions of human and AI ideas in the same dataset (PDF pp. 6–7, section 4.2).

studies.label: Food-waste brainstorming experiment: reanalysis of flexibility

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were assigned to human-only brainstorming or human+AI brainstorming. The experiment was conducted in three courses at the authors' university's informatics department. Course-based setting is coded field_rct under the codebook; classes were not the assignment unit (PDF p. 4, section 3.1; p. 5, section 4).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4, Results; setting and conditions: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is stated in the PDF.

arms.name: human+AI
arms.description: Individual brainstorming in the app with on-demand AI suggestions. Participants were asked to request suggestions at least once; suggestions appeared in a separate list and could be copied into the participant's own list. Only accepted suggestions counted toward the submitted result (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1–3.2). Analyzed arm count: PDF p. 5, section 4.

arms.name: human-only
arms.description: Individual brainstorming in the same study's baseline condition without generative-AI suggestions (PDF p. 4, section 3.1). Analyzed arm count: PDF p. 5, section 4.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 54 participants and excludes two students because of incomplete data and a misunderstanding of the task, leaving 52 analyzed. The timing of exclusions relative to random assignment and the excluded participants' arms are not stated. The total randomized count is therefore left null. Separately, seven unclassified ideas and all deleted ideas were excluded from idea analyses; these are output exclusions, not additional participant exclusions. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Sections 3.3 and 4.
participants.who: University students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs; recruited through the university's courses on design science research, computer-supported cooperative work, and data-driven solutions for the smart city. The document describes the university as Western European (PDF pp. 4–5, sections 3.1, 3.3 and 4).
participants.quote: The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4, Results, for people, exclusions and arm counts; PDF p. 4, section 3.1, for courses; PDF p. 5, section 3.3, for region and idea exclusions.

ai_tool.how_used: A custom brainstorming app supplied three AI ideas per request in a separate panel; participants could copy suggestions into their own list or use them as stimuli. Prompts incorporated the brainstorming question, the participant's ideas, and previous AI ideas; temperature was 0.9. This was on-demand supply of complete ideas rather than free-form chatbot use (PDF p. 4, section 3.2 and Figure 2; p. 5, opening paragraph).

task.description: Generate ideas addressing 'How can we reduce food waste?' Participants brainstormed individually, then selected their best ideas and completed a post-questionnaire. The scored flexibility outcomes concern brainstorming idea lists, not a separate assessment after AI removal (PDF p. 4, section 3.1; pp. 5–6, section 4.1).
task.duration: 10 minutes of brainstorming; about 30 minutes for the whole study (PDF p. 4, section 3.1).

outcomes.name: Flexibility of the submitted idea list, including accepted AI ideas (H1)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of distinct categories covered by each participant's idea list, using the predefined Specht and Buck system with 13 categories in five clusters. An assistant blind to condition categorized the ideas. The human+AI lists include 115 accepted/copied AI suggestions, not all 373 logged AI suggestions (PDF p. 5, section 3.3 and beginning of section 4.1; p. 6, section 4.1). Despite the paper's 'team' label, each observation is the list of one human participant, with or without AI.

contrasts.reported: human+AI mdn=5; human-only mdn=2; Mann-Whitney U=546.5, p<.001; rank-biserial correlation rB=.617. The text also reports mean=4.115 for category coverage without identifying it as an arm-specific mean. No arm SDs, SEs or CIs are printed; rB is the reported rank-biserial effect, not a standardized mean difference.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1 and Figure 3; inclusion of accepted AI ideas begins on PDF p. 5.

outcomes.name: Flexibility of human-authored ideas, excluding AI-origin ideas (H2)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct categories among each participant's human-authored ideas, excluding AI-origin ideas in the human+AI condition. The same category coding is used as for H1. Human-authored ideas in the treatment were generated while AI suggestions were available (PDF pp. 4–6). Figure 4 presents boxplots; unlabeled arm medians were not estimated from the graph.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U=326.0, p=.830; no significant between-condition difference. The text reports mean=2.846 for category coverage without identifying it as an arm-specific mean. No arm SDs, SEs or CIs are printed, and arm medians were not estimated from Figure 4. An accompanying association between human idea number and categories covered is reported as Spearman’s ρ=.817, p<.001; this is a correlation, not an AI-treatment effect.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, paragraphs surrounding Figure 4.

outcomes.name: Human within-category fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average number of human-authored ideas per category covered, calculated for each participant; participants contributing no ideas were assigned zero. This measures depth within the participant's categories, not similarity across people (PDF p. 6, section 4.1).

contrasts.reported: human-only mdn=2; human+ai mdn=1; Mann-Whitney U=119.0, p<.001. No arm SDs, SEs, CIs or standardized effect are printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, paragraph immediately before section 4.2.

outcomes.name: Number of human-authored ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Human-origin idea counts and participant means by randomized condition, excluding AI-origin ideas. Table 2 supplies means and total idea counts, and section 4 supplies analyzed arm sizes; SDs are absent. The statistics_available descriptor refers to the available arm descriptives only, not to a complete mean/SD/n package.

contrasts.reported: Table 2: human+AI human-origin ideas=87 (mean=3.3); human-only human-origin ideas=140 (mean=5.4); human-origin total=227. Section 4 reports 26 analyzed people per arm. Section 4.1 says human-only participants contributed significantly more ideas and refers to the earlier under-review study, but gives no quantity test statistic or p value. Section 5.1 instead says there was no significant difference in the number of human ideas. Direction reflects the printed means; the significance claim is internally inconsistent.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2 and section 4; PDF p. 6, section 4.1; conflicting statement on PDF p. 8 (printed p. 428), section 5.1.

outcomes.name: Total logged idea quantity, including all retained AI suggestions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Descriptive condition-level corpus totals in Table 2, combining human-origin ideas and all AI suggestions retained after output exclusions. These counts include suggestions not accepted into participants’ final lists; section 3.1 excludes unaccepted suggestions from participants’ results, and section 4.1 uses only the accepted/copied subset for flexibility. The full logged total is therefore coded other and scored_on_output=false, not participant-output fluency, and does not support eligibility criterion 3. The with_ai label records the assistance context; category_count and unit=set describe the logged corpus. Section 5.1 separately claims greater joint idea quantity but does not define the idea set or provide a test; it cannot be established whether that claim concerns final accepted lists or the full logged corpus. The qualitative claim is retained in reported without assigning its significance to the corpus totals (PDF p. 4, section 3.1; p. 5, Table 2; pp. 5–6, section 4.1; p. 7, section 5.1).

contrasts.reported: Table 2: human+AI total=460 ideas; human-only total=140 ideas; overall total=600 ideas. The human+AI corpus includes 373 AI-origin ideas (mean=14.3) and 87 human-origin ideas (mean=3.3); human-only has 140 human-origin ideas (mean=5.4). These are retained logged ideas, including unaccepted AI suggestions, not accepted final-list totals. Section 4.1 identifies 115 accepted/copied AI suggestions. Section 5.1 states that the human working with AI jointly produced significantly more ideas than alone, but gives no corresponding test statistic, p value, combined arm means or explicit accepted-versus-logged definition. It is unresolved which quantity supports that claim. The direction here describes the Table 2 totals only; their statistical significance is not established.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2 and section 4; PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 425–426), section 4.1, accepted suggestions; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 5.1, final paragraph on the page, joint-quantity claim.

outcomes.name: Pooled category coverage and distribution by human versus AI origin
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Descriptive category distribution and number of categories covered after pooling human-origin ideas across both randomized arms and AI-origin suggestions from the human+AI arm. Category-specific percentages are kept together as one distribution outcome. This compares interacting sources of ideas, not independent AI and human samples or similarity across different participants. Retained from screener B as a source-supported output measure with question=none. Figure 5 was inspected directly in a rendering of the PDF; its numerical labels are not present in the extracted PDF text.

contrasts.control_arm: Human-origin ideas pooled across human+AI and human-only sessions
contrasts.reported: AI ideas cover all 13 categories; human ideas cover 12, with none in value-added products (section 4.2). Corpus sizes in Table 2: AI=373 ideas, human=227 ideas. Figure 5 percentages, human then AI: converting food waste into energy 1,3% / 0,8%; family and consumer science training 1,8% / 6,4%; food date labeling 2,2% / 1,6%; food waste for agricultural purposes 1,8% / 7,0%; food waste markets 7,0% / 8,0%; large-scale food donation 10,1% / 14,5%; legislating food waste reduction 12,3% / 9,9%; meal planning 7,9% / 1,1%; mobile technology 2,2% / 13,4%; public information campaigns 11,9% / 11,5%; smart technology 4,4% / 8,3%; value-added products AI 0,5% (no human bar; human absence is stated in the text); waste mitigation 37,0% / 16,9%. Decimal commas are retained from Figure 5. No inferential test or uncertainty interval is reported.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), Figure 5 and accompanying paragraph; corpus counts: PDF p. 5, Table 2.

outcomes.name: Rate of introducing a new category after the brainstorming counterpart contributes
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Within human+AI sessions only, the authors chronologically ordered contributions and examined cases in which a human contributed after the AI or the AI contributed after the human. They report the fraction of contributions that explore new categories by source. The denominator of eligible contributions is not given, so n_units=null. This is a descriptive process comparison within the assisted condition, not a randomized arm contrast. It is coded with_ai because the contributions were produced while AI was available and the construct is other; categories are tracked within each participant’s session, not across different people (PDF p. 7, section 4.2).

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI contributions after human contributions, within human+AI sessions
contrasts.control_arm: Human contributions after AI contributions, within human+AI sessions
contrasts.reported: AI explores new categories in 41.2% of cases; humans explore new categories in 41.9% of cases. These are descriptive percentages; no denominator, test statistic, p value, SE or CI is reported. The discussion says both similarly drove exploration; no inferential equivalence is established.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 4.2, final paragraph; interpretation continues across PDF pp. 7–8, section 5.1.

eligibility.reason: Random assignment of individual students to human+AI versus human-only brainstorming is explicit (PDF p. 5, printed p. 425, section 4); GPT-3.5 suggestions were available while treatment participants generated ideas (PDF p. 4, printed p. 424, sections 3.1–3.2). The same experiment analyzed 52 people, 26 per arm, after two exclusions from 54 participants. This is close to, but meets, the 50-person threshold; assignment-stage counts remain null because exclusion timing and pre-exclusion arm counts are not stated (PDF p. 5, section 4). A condition-blind assistant categorized actual ideas, and S1-O1 and S1-O2 count categories within each participant’s submitted or human-authored idea list (PDF p. 5, section 3.3; pp. 5–6, section 4.1). Criterion 3 therefore remains met after excluding S1-O5’s full logged corpus from qualifying participant-output scores. S1-O7 is a descriptive with_ai process comparison and is not needed to establish eligibility. This reanalysis retains the original experiment’s field_rct design class and requires sample deduplication; it is not an independent new sample.

one_line_finding: Among 52 analyzed students, lists including accepted AI suggestions covered a median of 5 categories versus 2 without AI (U=546.5, p<.001, rank-biserial rB=.617), while human-origin category coverage showed no significant difference (U=326.0, p=.830; PDF p. 5, section 4; p. 6, section 4.1).
open_questions: Which publication is the earlier under-review study whose data were reused? The PDF establishes overlap but does not identify its title, full citation or eventual publication (PDF pp. 1 and 4, sections 1 and 3.2). Do not identify it from the unverified search-record lead.

What were the total and per-arm counts at random assignment, and when were the two participant exclusions applied? The paper gives overall participation and analyzed arm sizes, but no explicit pre-exclusion allocation counts (PDF p. 5, section 4).

Which statement about the significance of human-origin idea quantity is correct? Section 4.1 says human-only participants contributed significantly more ideas (PDF p. 6), whereas section 5.1 says no significant difference was observed (PDF p. 8); no numerical test for this quantity comparison is printed.

What idea set, analysis unit and inferential statistics support the joint-quantity claim in section 5.1 (PDF p. 7, final paragraph)? The PDF does not link that claim explicitly to accepted final lists or to Table 2’s logged corpus.

Are participant-level arm SDs, SEs or confidence intervals for the flexibility and fluency contrasts available in an identified report or dataset? They are not printed here, and no supplement or data repository is identified.
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09 against the current codebook and form spec, all 380 lines of the markdown conversion including references, text extracted from all 10 PDF pages, and all three c861 challenge files. No appendix is present or supplement identified. Recorded numbers were checked against the PDF; Figures 3–5 were inspected in memory, including every recorded Figure 5 percentage. Both outcome-lens problems were confirmed and corrected. S1-O5 retains the printed logged-corpus counts as descriptive context with construct=other and scored_on_output=false; the full corpus includes unaccepted AI suggestions and is not participant-output fluency. S1-O7 is now with_ai because new-category contributions were made during assisted sessions. Its source/process comparison remains descriptive, with no randomized assistance contrast or reported denominator or uncertainty. Seven entries are retained, including the descriptive corpus and source comparisons. S1-O6 remains question=none because it compares pooled human-origin ideas with AI suggestions, with mixed AI availability for the human-origin pool. The separate section 5.1 joint-quantity significance claim remains unresolved; no accepted joint total, combined mean, effect size or precision was calculated. The conflicting human-quantity significance statements are preserved. H1 and H2 remain paper_primary as the paper’s explicit hypotheses; no preregistration or unique primary-outcome ranking is stated (PDF p. 4). The main category scores are flexibility within each participant’s list, not across_people diversity. Human-origin ideas were produced while AI remained available, so removing AI-origin ideas from scoring does not create an after_ai outcome. The 373 logged AI suggestions and 115 accepted/copied suggestions are distinct (PDF pp. 5–6), and idea counts are not people counts. All post-exclusion people counts are described as analyzed, with randomized counts left null. The reanalysis retains field_rct from the original course-based experiment (PDF p. 4), with individual assignment (PDF p. 5). Country remains not_stated; affiliation is not substituted for a stated participant country. No preregistration, supplement, public data/code URL, or original-study bibliographic identity is identified in this PDF. Novelty and value are described as the earlier study’s focus without corresponding outcome statistics here; subjective perceptions and request frequency do not establish criterion 3. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical review evidence; final.challenge_resolution records the subsequent coding corrections. All five open_questions are triaged in final.open_items; its fourth entry also covers the one unresolved reconciliation difference. None affects the three eligibility criteria. The final resolution counters count challenged problems, not the separate open reporting items.

a.name: Joint human-and-AI idea quantity
a.measure_detail: The discussion reports joint idea quantity for the human+AI condition versus the human-only condition. No numerical contrast or complete definition of this quantity analysis is printed. Section 3.1 says only ideas in the participant's list count toward results, and Section 4.1 identifies the accepted AI subset. Table 2 includes all analyzed AI suggestions and therefore cannot be read as the final accepted joint output count. Retained because it is an output-based quantity result explicitly reported by the paper. PDF pp. 4-7 (printed pp. 424-427), Sections 3.1, 4, 4.1 and 5.1.
a.reported: Section 5.1 states that the human working with the AI jointly produced significantly more ideas than alone. No numerical effect, arm means for accepted joint output, test statistic or p-value accompanies this claim. Table 2's human+AI total of 460 includes 373 AI suggestions and 87 human ideas; Section 4.1 says 115 AI suggestions were accepted/copied. No final joint count or effect has been calculated here.
a.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), Section 5.1, final paragraph; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2; PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 425-426), Section 4.1.

b.name: Total logged idea quantity, including all retained AI suggestions
b.measure_detail: Descriptive condition-level corpus counts from Table 2, combining human-origin ideas and all retained AI suggestions. These are not counts of final accepted idea lists: all retained AI suggestions enter this table, whereas the main flexibility analysis uses only accepted/copied suggestions. The table aggregates ideas within each condition; no combined participant mean or variance is given.
b.reported: Table 2: human+AI total=460 ideas; human-only total=140 ideas; overall total=600 ideas. The human+AI corpus includes 373 AI-origin ideas (mean=14.3) and 87 human-origin ideas (mean=3.3). Section 5.1 states that humans with AI jointly produced significantly more ideas, but no corresponding test statistic or p value is printed. These are idea counts, not people or counts of accepted final outputs.
b.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), opening of section 5.1; accepted-suggestion distinction: PDF pp. 5–6, section 4.1.

differences.resolved: Retain the Table 2 corpus totals as a descriptive logged-quantity outcome and retain the section 5.1 joint-quantity claim with an explicit limitation. The corpus totals are confirmed, and they include unaccepted suggestions. Neither form can establish which idea set or inferential analysis underlies the significance claim. Its accepted-versus-logged definition, analysis unit and test statistics remain unknown; no accepted joint total or treatment effect is supplied.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O5 construct/scored_on_output: the full logged corpus was coded as participant-output fluency despite including unaccepted AI suggestions.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Changed construct from fluency to other and scored_on_output from true to false. Retained the verified Table 2 counts, category_count measure and set unit as descriptive corpus information. Clarified that the with_ai label records assistance context only and that this entry does not support criterion 3. The undocumented joint-quantity significance claim remains separate and unresolved; eligibility rests on other participant-level output scores.
challenge_resolution.quote: only suggestions in the “list of ideas” (left side of the screen) would count toward their results (i.e., not-accepted AI ideas are excluded).
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1, final paragraph; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2; PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 425–426), section 4.1, 115 accepted/copied suggestions. Codebook sections 3 and 6.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O7 question: new-category contributions produced within assisted sessions were coded none.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Changed question from none to with_ai and updated measure_detail. AI was available during these sessions, and the other construct tracks categories within a participant’s session. Retained the descriptive within-arm source/process comparison, output unit, and reported percentages; no randomized assistance effect or inferential equivalence is asserted.
challenge_resolution.quote: This analysis can only be carried out for the human+AI condition.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 4.2, paragraph beginning “We thus additionally take a process perspective”; AI availability: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), sections 3.1–3.2. Codebook section 1 and form-spec question field note.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Identify the earlier under-review study whose data were reused (PDF pp. 1 and 4, sections 1 and 3.2). Authors’ confirmation of its full citation and shared sample would settle deduplication. Its unidentified publication does not alter any of the three eligibility criteria for this experiment.

open_questions[1]: Confirm total and per-arm randomized counts, excluded participants’ arms, and exclusion timing (PDF p. 5, section 4). Authors’ allocation and participant-flow records would settle this. Random assignment and 52 analyzed people are already explicit, so criteria 1 and 2 remain met.

open_questions[2]: Resolve the conflicting significance claims for human-origin idea quantity in sections 4.1 and 5.1 (PDF pp. 6 and 8). Authors’ correction and the underlying quantity test would settle which statement is correct. Eligibility requires a scored output, not a statistically significant effect, so no criterion depends on this discrepancy.

open_questions[3] and unresolved reconciliation.differences[0]: Identify the idea set, analysis unit and inferential statistics behind the section 5.1 joint-quantity claim (PDF p. 7). Authors’ specification of accepted-versus-logged ideas and their original analysis would settle it. S1-O5 is now descriptive corpus information; participant-level flexibility scores independently satisfy criterion 3.

open_questions[4]: Obtain participant-level arm SDs, SEs or confidence intervals for flexibility and fluency (PDF pp. 5–6). No supplement or public data repository is identified; authors would need to supply the missing statistics or underlying participant-level scores. This concerns effect extraction and precision, not any of the three eligibility criteria.
